title: About Methylene Blue dye and DIY recording plates

posts.topic_title: About Methylene Blue dye and DIY recording plates
posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.post_subject: About Methylene Blue dye and DIY recording plates
posts.content_md:
Methylene Blue is in the family of dyes known as Thiazine dyes (includes Rose Bengal). 

As Martin says when hit with light they can become oxidants and this is opposite to what one tries trying to achieve by getting light to break down silver bromide grains so that silver can recover its missing electron and return to being silver metal. (It had lost its outer electron becoming bound to bromine to make Br- ion.in the first place)

So in other words MB is a desensitizer of AgBr grains.

Interestingly when methylene blue dyed film is hit by red light in the right damp environment it does loose its colour and becomes bleached (known as leuco MB) So this leuco form is then a reducing agent and it will seek to give back its newly aquired electrons either to ariel oxygen slowly or almost instantly if there is a good oxidant around such as dichromate. So with dichromate present it won’t appear to bleach and still retains its strong blue colour all the time .[Appl. Optics ,Vol 30. no.13 May 1991]

So this then changes the dichromate to “Chromium 3” and this stuff is in effect like chrome alum and hardens gelatin. So that in essence is how it helps to make red sensitive DCG’s. 

 Over 10 years ago I actually managed to make holograms using just bleached methylene blue in a very thick layer of PVA (0.5-1 mm) The holograms were able to demonstrate real time interference they were VERY feeble and only lasted a minute or two. They were made with the simplest possible transmission set up --virtually a single beam with an anodized aluminium block with some black writing on it next to the MeBlue recording plate all illuminated together by spread beam from a HeNe . laser . After leaving the stablized set-up under .laser illumination for about 2 mins 

and then removing the block you could still clearly see the image of the block still there existing only as a bleached Me Blue image. ( It was best to illuminate it for viewing under the laser by cutting down the laser intensity with a bit of filter so that the image would last for longer.) I gave a piece of this special plate to Graham Saxby and he was able to make fleeting interference fringes on a solid coffee cup when he touched it and wrote it up as an observation in our RPS newsletter some years ago. The used plate was then put in a dark place and it oxidized itself back to its full blue colour in a day or two –ready to be used again.. –No wet processing or other treatments required. These plates could still be used years later but they were spoilt often by moulds growing on them in patches, (It was essential to have moisturizers in the material for them to work,) . Gelatin did not work at all well though which is why I chose PVA. . No-I’m afraid I never managed to make a visible reflection hologram with it.

I will do a note on my experience on using PVA for the AgBr diffusion system later.

Thanks Jeff & Martin for your lucid replies. I find Danny's suggestion intriguing - expose MB SH hologram with red light, then flash with incoherent

short-wavelength light and develop to get anti-fringes. I expect this would be pretty inefficient - I think it would take a lot more light energy to inhibit the SH grain development than it would to trigger it since there is no inherent amplification mechanism. But it would be interesting if it worked at all....

posts.author: Martin
posts.post_subject: About Methylene Blue dye and DIY recording plates
posts.content_md:
> **Tom B.:** Thanks Jeff & Martin for your lucid replies. I find Danny's suggestion intriguing - expose MB SH hologram with red light, then flash with incoherentshort-wavelength light and develop to get anti-fringes. I expect this would be pretty inefficient - I think it would take a lot more light energy to inhibit the SH grain development than it would to trigger it since there is no inherent amplification mechanism. But it would be interesting if it worked at all....

Sergio and I did make some attempts in that direction in the hope of getting some SHSG type of hologram. I don't recall the details anymore, but I think we exposed-developed-reversal bleached a piece of 8E75 film. We then sensitized the emulsion in a MB/TEA solution and re-exposed it to strong incoherent light. I believe the film was subsequently put in a 0,5% am. dichr. solution and kept under dark and humid condition for several hours. Ultimately, the emulsion was developed/dried a la DCG. The results were disapointing. I suspect - once more - the emulsion's "prehistory" (that's to say, its hardening) is paramount for this kind of experiments.

posts.content_md:
[
> Thanks for chiming in Jeff, the AgBr/PVA note will be of interest.What about Azure A, my Merck lists an absorption max at 620 - 624nm and I've got an unreferenced note here indicating that it's peak is at 633nm. Is it as pointless in silver emulsions as MB? Any better in DCG?-Gary]

Yes that Azure A looks like it should be best Gary. 

The fastest fading dye was the the simplest one in the series--

thionine, - It was however too good and didnt recover in the dark. 

I notice that the formula for Azure A is half MB and half thionine. Maybe just the job. 

The important trick I developed to get the photosensitivity up and give a demo to a class-room of kids was to add an amine. So I put a sheet of heavily MB dyed film in front of a 100W bulb with a photographic positive transparency over it and after 10 secs the thing could be taken away and viewed as a blue and white transparency. 

An amine combination worked best such as triethanolamine approximately neutralized with EDTA (that is the free acid not the sodium salt of EDTA) in the PVA film.

I think I will get some Azure A in and give it a go and write it up for 

Kaveh's Holographer.org. It would be great if some of you porcelaincateers picked it up and ran with it--improved it as a fun demo

and for possibly even for serious interferometry 

Thank you for those ideas there might be some others worth trying too.

Jeff

> **Dinesh:** jeff-blyth wrote:Interestingly when methylene blue dyed film is hit by red light in the right damp environment it does loose its colour and becomes bleached (known as leuco MB) So this leuco form is then a reducing agent and it will seek to give back its newly aquired electrons either to ariel oxygen slowly or almost instantly if there is a good oxidant around such as dichromate.What about grains with specks on them. Will the leuco form of MB act as a developer to silver halide when exposed to red light?

You could use a leuco dye MB solution that was reduced by means of an electron donor and try develop (reduce) the silver halide as an usual way, but the oxidized leuco dye returns to the high blue stain again and you need to remove this stain from the emulsion.

> I notice that the formula for Azure A is half MB and half thionine.

Hmm, I'm definitely no chemist, but from what I see in the Merck the Azure A looks like it's own molecule with several similarly named variations that include it along with other stuff (methylene blue and it's oxidation products, etc). As always I'll be interested to see what you have to say about it.

On another note, has anyone ever produced a "kit" for the DIY plates? The actual chemicals required for about 25 4x5 inch plates as per your DIY page would cost less than $8, or as little as about $5 with some diligence. If existing photgraphic materials were used to supply a pre-applied emulsion (whether backed by glass or otherwise) then it should be possible to produce a kit at a price that would make it worthwhile to the buyer to purchase as well as for the seller to spend the time putting it together(25 4x5 sheets of DIY holo-material for $25 - $35? That would be ~100 quarter sheets). Hmm. I wonder what the annual market for that would be? A few dozen to a couple hundred? If it worked well enough there'd be repeat buyers and a larger more economical "kit" could be worked up.

Cripes, I gotta get some pinacyanol in here!

	-Gary
